title: AI Debt ETFs Launch as Firms Package Credit Default Swaps
summary: Tuttle Capital and Defiance ETFs file to launch leveraged funds tracking AI credit risk via CDS on CoreWeave, Oracle, Meta. Retail bet on default fears.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Two firms filed with the SEC to launch ETFs tracking credit default swaps on AI companies CoreWeave, Oracle, and Meta.
- The leveraged funds let retail investors bet on rising default risk as AI debt concerns spike following a 15% Nasdaq correction.
- Oracle CDS volumes hit a record $47.6 billion amid fears that AI infrastructure spending outpaces revenue growth potential.


Two investment firms are bringing credit default swap exposure to retail investors through new exchange-traded funds targeting artificial intelligence infrastructure companies. Tuttle Capital Management and Defiance ETFs each filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on November 10, 2026, proposing leveraged funds tied to credit risk at CoreWeave, Oracle, and Meta Platforms. The filings arrive as AI stocks face one of their sharpest selloffs in years, with the Nasdaq down 15% from its October peak through early November.


## Officially Launched on November 10, 2026


The SEC filings were submitted on November 10, 2026, marking the official launch of the regulatory approval process. Tuttle Capital is proposing five actively managed ETFs that effectively let retail investors buy leveraged credit protection on AI-related companies. Defiance plans to offer four similarly structured ETFs. Each fund is designed to rise when the issuer's debt profile deteriorates and credit spreads widen, or fall if the outlook brightens and spreads narrow. The products would compete with short selling and options as tools for betting against AI stocks.


## Targeting CoreWeave, Oracle, and Meta Credit Risk


The proposed ETFs focus on individual companies at the center of AI infrastructure spending. Oracle holds the weakest credit rating among major hyperscalers and has become a proxy for AI debt risk. Its five-year credit default swaps hit a record last month as investors feared a post-earnings borrowing spree would overwhelm debt markets. Oracle later disclosed plans for just $10 billion of gross debt growth through fiscal 2030, easing some concerns. CoreWeave, a neocloud provider, has tapped both high-yield and loan markets with multi-billion dollar deals to finance its buildout. CoreWeave CDS contracts currently price in a more than 60% chance of default within five years, with trading volumes reaching $4.6 billion from just $145 million earlier in 2026. Meta Platforms rounds out the target list, despite carrying an investment-grade credit rating.


## Credit Default Swaps Meet Retail Investors


Credit default swaps, derivatives typically used by institutions to hedge against default, gained wider attention during the 2008 financial crisis. ProShares launched the first CDS ETFs in 2014, but those products struggled and eventually closed. The new offerings differ by targeting individual companies and a specific sector under scrutiny. According to Barclays credit strategist Jigar Patel, Oracle CDS are now the most active single-name contract in the US market at a record $47.6 billion, up from $8.7 billion through October 30, 2026. Trading volumes for CDS tied to the 10 largest hyperscalers and chipmakers have reached record highs, making them some of the most actively traded US contracts outside the financial sector.


## Leveraged Structure Amplifies Risk and Returns


The proposed funds plan to use borrowed money to amplify returns, magnifying both gains and losses. Investors could wind up losing money even if the targeted company's shares are plunging, because the ongoing cost of maintaining CDS protection eats away at returns before credit damage occurs. Bloomberg Intelligence analyst James Seyffart expressed skepticism about retail adoption due to complexity, though he noted that a deeper AI selloff could change the calculus. Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas, said the moment fits the product but cautioned that CDS is not a common instrument and has been tried before with limited success.


## AI Infrastructure Spending Under Scrutiny


The AI trade unraveled in recent weeks as investors grew concerned that enormous spending on the technology could take years to pay off. Democrats' sweeping congressional victory in November 2026 raised the prospect of tighter regulation, further weighing on sentiment. Demand for credit protection has pushed CDS prices tied to hyperscalers and chipmakers to fresh highs from almost nonexistent a year ago. CoreWeave's talk of tapping vast pools of capital from insurers spooked investors last month, sending its CDS to an all-time high. Representatives for Oracle, Meta, and CoreWeave did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the ETF filings.


## What This Means


The launch of CDS-linked ETFs targeting AI infrastructure companies signals Wall Street's recognition of rising default concerns in a sector that has attracted unprecedented capital. While the products face adoption hurdles due to their complexity and the mixed track record of earlier CDS ETFs, they offer retail investors a new tool to hedge against or profit from AI debt risks. With Oracle CDS volumes surging to record levels and CoreWeave contracts pricing in significant default probability, the timing aligns with a moment of heightened anxiety about whether AI spending will generate sufficient returns to service mounting debt loads. Whether these funds succeed will depend on both the depth of any AI selloff and retail investors' willingness to embrace derivatives that once played a central role in the global financial crisis.
